articles.title: Screening for Health-Related Social Needs at Mammography Encounters and Subsequent Breast Imaging Adherence.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Health-related social needs (HRSNs), such as food insecurity or transportation difficulties, may affect breast cancer screening and follow-up. We assessed the use of screening mammography (SM) encounters to identify HRSNs and the association between the presence of any HRSN and adherence to recommended breast imaging. METHODS: Women presenting for SM received an optional questionnaire assessing desire for assistance with 8 HRSNs. Demographic and imaging data were extracted for each respondent. Multivariable logistic regression identified factors independently associated with adherence. RESULTS: 86% (1463/1704) of women completed the questionnaire, of whom 244 (17%) reported ≥1 HRSN. HRSNs were more common with younger age (p=0.0009), as well as non-White race, Hispanic/Latino ethnicity, non-English primary language, and Medicaid/MassHealth (all p<0.0001). Among women with BI-RADS 1 or 2 index SMs, subsequent SM adherence was lower with ≥1 HRSN (73% vs 87%; p<0.0001). Among women with BI-RADS 0 index SMs, diagnostic imaging adherence was 76% with ≥1 HRSN compared with 95% without HRSNs (p=0.05). On multivariable analysis, ≥1 HRSN was independently associated with lower odds of breast imaging adherence (aOR, 0.57; 95% CI, 0.40-0.83). Among women who completed recommended imaging, median (IQR) time to follow-up did not differ by HRSN status for BI-RADS 1 or 2 (366 [363,370] vs 366 [364,378] days; p=0.16) or BI-RADS 0 (30 [15,37] vs 30 [13,130] days; p=0.61). CONCLUSIONS: SM encounters can be used to identify HRSNs. Women reporting ≥1 HRSN were less likely to adhere to breast imaging recommendations, suggesting that HRSN screening during mammography may identify women at increased risk of non-adherence.

articles.title: Boundary-Ambiguity-Aware Lesion Evidence Learning for Breast Ultrasound Segmentation and Multimodal Classification.
articles.abstract: Multimodal analysis of breast ultrasound images and structured clinical data can support lesion characterization across diverse clinical classification tasks. However, existing image and clinicopathological data fusion methods usually fuse imaging and clinical information as feature vectors, without explicitly organizing ultrasound-derived evidence according to anatomical roles such as the lesion core, ambiguous boundary and peritumoral tissue. Therefore, this paper proposes a boundary-ambiguity-aware lesion evidence learning framework (BAA-LEL) for joint breast ultrasound lesion segmentation and multimodal classification. BAA-LEL first extracts a lesion prior with a MedSAM-assisted segmentation branch and refines ambiguous margins through an anchor-constrained boundary graph. The refined lesion prior is organized into core, boundary, and peritumoral regions, while boundary geometry and ambiguity are retained as complementary evidence. A morphology-clinical heterogeneous graph then models interactions among regional morphology, boundary evidence, and structured clinical variables for task-specific classification. Experiments on HER2USC, LNMUSC, BrEaST, BUSI, and ISIC IMA++ demonstrate strong segmentation performance and competitive classification performance across breast ultrasound and cross-domain settings. Controlled ablations, statistical comparisons, calibration analysis, and interpretability experiments further support the contributions of boundary-aware refinement, zonal morphology encoding, and morphology-clinical heterogeneous reasoning. The source code is available at: https://github.com/JinlinYY/BAA-LEL.

articles.title: Can CT Phantoms Produce Realistic CT Images of Human Anatomy? Physics-Based Evaluation of Multimaterial 3D-Printed CT Phantoms From CT Data.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Patient-specific computed tomography (CT) phantoms can be produced using a novel 3D-printing technique that aims at replicating measured CT image volumes with high anatomic fidelity and accurate CT values. The purpose of this study is a comprehensive physics-based evaluation of both technical phantoms and a full-size adult abdominal phantom with regard to image-quality metrics and the reproducibility of CT values. In addition, the visualization of abdominal pathologies will be assessed. MATERIALS AND METHODS: The study was conducted in 3 steps. First, a geometric reference disc phantom (40 mm thickness, 150 mm diameter) was 3D-printed using multimaterial jetting and scanned on a commercial photon-counting detector CT (PCD-CT) to assess the CT values of the base materials used for printing and to evaluate the influence of the printing process on spatial resolution and noise properties. Second, CT images of the reference phantom reconstructed with a medium-sharp and a sharp kernel were used as templates to print 2 CT-derived disc phantoms using multimaterial jetting with voxel-based material mapping. These phantoms were then scanned to assess how template image sharpness propagates into the image-quality properties of the final printed phantoms. Spatial resolution was evaluated using edge spread function (ESF) analysis and edge rise distance (ERD), whereas noise characteristics were assessed using noise power spectrum (NPS) analysis. Third, as a proof of concept, a full-size adult abdominal phantom was 3D-printed with a patient CT data set as template. Phantom images were compared with patient images regarding CT values, spatial resolution, noise properties, and the depiction of pathologic structures. RESULTS: Evaluation of the CT attenuation of the base materials showed that CT values ranging from -37 HU to 995 HU in virtual monoenergetic images at 60 keV can be printed.For the reference disc, measured ESF curves showed close agreement with theoretical expectations across all reconstruction kernels, indicating preservation of spatial resolution by the printing process. CT-derived discs showed minor edge smoothing compared with the reference for smooth and medium-sharp reconstructions. For sharp reconstructions, edge smoothing was severe, with an ERD increase of up to 32% compared with the reference. Edge smoothing was more pronounced for the disc based on a sharp template. NPS were highly consistent across all discs, with only minor differences in peak amplitude. In the abdominal phantom images ESF and NPS closely matched those of the patient CT images. Measured attenuation agreed well for tissues with positive CT values up to 1000 HU. Fat was represented with increased CT values because of print material limitations. Clinically relevant pathologic structures, including a large hepatocellular carcinoma and a smaller focal liver lesion, were displayed comparably in the phantom images. CONCLUSIONS: CT phantoms generated from CT image volumes using 3D printing with multimaterial mapping on a voxel level accurately reproduce the template images in terms of image sharpness, noise characteristics, and attenuation properties of tissues with positive CT values not exceeding 1000 HU. The achievable spatial resolution is limited to medium-sharp levels and does not improve by using sharper template images. These findings support the use of image-based multimaterial 3D printing to produce realistic anthropomorphic phantoms for advanced CT image-quality assessment and optimization, and for validation of reconstruction algorithms and quantitative CT imaging methods.

articles.title: Multi-Site Quality Assurance of ADC and PDFF Measurements: A Multi-Vendor Phantom Study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Reliable quantitative imaging biomarkers are important for multi-site studies. However, scanner- and site-specific variations can compromise the clinical utility of many measures including apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) and proton density fat fraction (PDFF). Phantom-based quality assurance provides a foundation for multi-site studies. PURPOSE: To evaluate cross-site reproducibility, intra-session reliability, and accuracy of ADC and PDFF measurements across four sites. STUDY TYPE: Prospective phantom study. PHANTOMS: A NIST diffusion phantom (CaliberMRI, Model 128) and a fat phantom (Calimetrix, Model 300). FIELD STRENGTH/SEQUENCE: 3 T/diffusion-weighted spin-echo echo-planar imaging for ADC and 3D gradient-echo imaging for PDFF. ASSESSMENT: ADC and PDFF were measured to assess cross-site reproducibility and intra-session reliability. Accuracy was evaluated against reference values. STATISTICAL TESTS: Intra-session repeatability was assessed using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). Intra-session measurement variability was quantified using the coefficient of variation (CoV), and agreement between repeated measurements was assessed using Lin's concordance correlation coefficient (LCCC). NRMSE (normalized root mean square error) assessed accuracy relative to reference values. A linear mixed-effects (LME) model assessed site differences in ADC and PDFF, with p < 0.05 considered statistically significant, while two one-sided tests (TOST) assessed equivalence within prespecified margins of ±10% for ADC and ±5% for PDFF. RESULTS: ICC demonstrated excellent repeatability across repeated scans for both ADC and PDFF (ICC > 0.99). Mean NRMSE between measured and reference values was < 10.0% for ADC and < 7.0% for PDFF, suggesting high accuracy. Mean intra-session CoV was < 1.0% for ADC and < 2.0% for PDFF, while LCCC exceeded 0.99 for both measurements, demonstrating strong agreement. LME models showed significant site effects for both ADC (F(3, 36) = 6.05) and PDFF (F(3, 33) = 5.07), while pairwise differences met the prespecified equivalence criteria for both measures. DATA CONCLUSION: Diffusion and fat phantoms provide reliable quality assurance tools for quantitative ADC and PDFF measurements across multiple MRI sites, supporting consistency despite statistically significant site effects. EVIDENCE LEVEL: 4. TECHNICAL EFFICACY: Stage 1.

articles.title: Broadband gamma-band EEG changes during magnetophosphene-inducing 20 Hz magnetic field stimulation.
articles.abstract: Magnetophosphenes are visual percepts induced by extremely low-frequency magnetic fields (ELF-MF; <300 Hz), yet the EEG expression of suprathreshold magnetophosphene-inducing stimulation remains poorly characterized and is not reliably captured by classical low-frequency markers. We tested whether suprathreshold 20 Hz tAMS is accompanied by broadband high-frequency EEG changes rather than focal oscillatory effects. EEG was recorded in N=13 healthy volunteers during 20 Hz sinusoidal magnetic-field exposure delivered using transcranial alternating magnetic stimulation (tAMS) in a global-head configuration. Three conditions were analyzed: no exposure (0 mT), subthreshold (5 mT), and suprathreshold (50 mT). Gamma-band EEG power (30-80 Hz) was quantified using complementary spectral approaches, including aperiodic-adjusted gamma power. Perception reports sharply dissociated the three conditions, with frequent perception at 50 mT only. Suprathreshold stimulation was associated with spatially distributed increases in gamma-band EEG power over frontal and occipito-parietal electrodes. The differences remained partly detectable in complementary analyses using two local aperiodic-adjustment methods and did not exhibit a consistent narrowband peak, a pattern consistent with broadband high-frequency changes. No focal power change over primary occipital electrodes remained significant after Bonferroni correction. These findings identify a spatially distributed broadband high-frequency scalp EEG effect associated with the suprathreshold 50 mT condition, with the main spatial pattern strongly preserved after ICA-based removal of components classified as ocular or muscular. The effect therefore characterizes the coupled suprathreshold stimulation-perception condition; its perception specificity and physiological source remain unresolved.

articles.title: SPARC: Sectorized Partial-Angle Reconstruction Based Motion Correction Method for Multi-Phase CCTA.
articles.abstract: Multi-phase Coronary Computed Tomography Angiography (CCTA) provides a clear visualization of coronary arteries, offering comprehensive and reliable imaging support for the clinical diagnosis of coronary artery disease. However, traditional motion correction reconstruction algorithms lack reconstruction robustness despite their interpretability, while deep learning reconstruction methods achieve high imaging quality at the expense of interpretability and anatomical reliability in clinical CCTA practice. This study aims to simultaneously achieve interpretable and robust multi-phase coronary reconstruction.Approach. We propose a motion trajectory estimation and motion correction framework termed sectorized partial-angle reconstruction-based motion correction (SPARC) for CCTA. The proposed framework integrates sectorized partial-angle reconstructions, a spatio-temporal cascaded network for coronary centerline extraction, and a phase-accumulated fuzzy C-means clustering algorithm for motion trajectory estimation. These components work together to minimize motion estimation errors and enhance the quality of motion-corrected reconstruction.Main results. Experimental results from both simulations and clinical studies demonstrate that SPARC achieves superior reconstruction performance compared with existing methods. SPARC effectively reduces coronary motion artifacts and restores clear vessel structures while preserving reconstruction fidelity, achieving the best scores on all metrics.Significance. By preserving both interpretability and anatomical reliability while effectively reducing motion artifacts, SPARC provides a clinically deployable solution for motion-corrected multi-phase CCTA, supporting more reliable imaging for coronary artery disease diagnosis.

articles.title: Artificial intelligence for cerebrovascular digital subtraction angiography: methods, evidence, and challenges.
articles.abstract: Cerebrovascular diseases remain a major cause of mortality and long-term disability worldwide. Digital subtraction angiography (DSA) provides high-spatiotemporal-resolution visualization of cerebrovascular anatomy and contrast-agent dynamics and plays an important role in diagnosis, interventional treatment planning, and treatment assessment. Artificial intelligence (AI) has increasingly been applied to cerebrovascular DSA, yet the available evidence is distributed across diverse imaging settings, technical tasks, datasets, and validation strategies. This structured topical review provides a DSA-centered overview of AI-assisted cerebrovascular image analysis across 2D DSA, three-dimensional rotational angiography, and four-dimensional DSA. Literature from Web of Science Core Collection and major engineering databases was screened at title, abstract, and full-text levels using predefined eligibility criteria. The literature is organized around six interconnected tasks: image preprocessing, vessel and lesion segmentation, image registration, reconstruction and generation, disease diagnosis and detection, and hemodynamic analysis. Representative conventional and learning-based methods are reviewed together with their datasets, evaluation metrics, validation designs, and available data or code resources, with particular attention to the strength and limitations of the supporting evidence. Recent studies demonstrate increasing use of spatiotemporal modeling, deep learning, and image-generation techniques, but clinical translation remains constrained by small or single-center datasets, heterogeneous acquisition protocols and evaluation practices, limited external and prospective validation, model interpretability, and deployment requirements. Future work should emphasize acquisition-aware and physics-informed modeling, multicenter and privacy-preserving collaboration, clinically meaningful validation, and closer integration with neurointerventional workflows. By linking methodological developments with their supporting evidence and translational challenges, this review aims to support the development of more robust and clinically applicable AI methods for cerebrovascular DSA.

articles.title: Experimental Validation of Skull Acoustic Modelling Strategies for Transcranial Focused Ultrasound Simulation: A Cross-Comparison Study.
articles.abstract: ObjectiveAccurate acoustic modelling of the skull is important for simulation-guided transcranial focused ultrasound (tFUS) applications. However, existing skull parameterization strategies vary widely in complexity and reported accuracy. This study systematically evaluates commonly used modelling approaches to determine their predictive performance across multiple frequencies and skull types.ApproachFive skull modelling strategies were assessed: two voxel-wise linear mapping models, one with fixed attenuation coefficient and one with Hounsfield unit (HU)-dependent attenuation coefficients; two three-layer models with fixed and skull-density ratio (SDR) dependent attenuation coefficient; and one single-layer fixed-parameter model. Nineteen regions of interest from five historical and two Thiel-embalmed human skulls were examined at 220 kHz, 680 kHz and 1000 kHz, bowl-surface source fields were reconstructed using holography, and intracranial pressure distributions were captured with a needle hydrophone. Measurements were compared with k-Wave simulations.ResultsAverage simulated peak pressure errors (ɛp) ranged from 20% to 31% across frequencies, whereas intensity errors (ɛI) reached 41% to 81%. Errors in -6 dB focal volume ranged from 18% to 65%, and focal position discrepancies were typically several millimeters. Simulation generally predicted smaller insertion losses than measured, indicating a tendency to underestimate skull-related attenuation and overestimate transmitted intracranial exposure. Among the five modelling strategies, the model with the lowest observed error varied with frequency and outcome. Paired specimen-level comparisons did not establish a consistent accuracy advantage for any strategy.SignificanceThese results indicate that current skull modelling strategies may reproduce the gross intracranial beam pattern while still misestimating the delivered acoustic exposure, focal coverage and localization. Such errors are directly relevant to tFUS dose selection, target coverage and safety-margin interpretation, underscoring the need for refined parameterization methods for reliable tFUS treatment planning.&#xD.

articles.title: Sampling-free Monte Carlo dropout approximation for single-pass uncertainty quantification in deep learning-based PET reconstructions.
articles.abstract: Medical image reconstructions using deep learning (DL) can rapidly generate high-quality images from degraded measurements, but their clinical adoption remains challenging, largely due to the lack of fast and reliable methods to quantify aleatoric (data-driven) and epistemic (model-driven) uncertainties on a per-prediction basis. We aim to develop a computationally efficient approach for estimating both uncertainties at the voxel level in DL-based image reconstruction within a single inference run.Approach: We present a moment propagation-based framework that analytically approximates the conventional, multi-realization Monte Carlo (MC) dropout by propagating feature-map means and marginal variances through network layers, followed by a pre-calibrated correction table to compensate for covariance effects omitted in the approximation. This enables joint estimation of reconstruction, aleatoric uncertainty and epistemic uncertainty in a single forward pass. The proposed framework was implemented on top of FastPET -- a network model synthesizing PET reconstructions from time-of-flight histo-images -- and evaluated in a patient pilot study of 26 total-body PET/CT acquisitions (16 [18F]-FDG and 10 [18F]-PSMA cases).Main Results: Proposed method achieved relatively strong agreement with the 50-pass MC approach, with absolute differences <0.5% for reconstruction, <4.2% for aleatoric uncertainty and <9.8% for epistemic uncertainty, along with narrow spreads across patients and tracer types, while reducing computation time by ~40-fold. In a complementary proof-of-concept low-count experiment, regional tracer uptake confidence intervals (CIs, derived from propagated uncertainties) widened with increased noise level, and reference uptakes consistently fell close to CI boundaries, indicating the proposed method could provide roughly calibrated uncertainty magnitudes reflecting quantitative prediction errors.Significance: The proposed approach provides a sampling-free and relatively accurate approximation to the multi-pass MC-based uncertainty estimation in the histo-image-based DL PET reconstruction framework. Per-prediction uncertainty quantification enables direct assessment of AI confidence and potentially supports more reliable and informed decision-making.

articles.title: Per-Bundle Statistical Limits and Learned-Prior Inversion in Multiplexed X-ray Imaging, with Application to Temporal CT.
articles.abstract: Temporal computed tomography (TCT) fires N_S=3 X-ray sources simultaneously onto a shared detector, creating a pre-reconstruction inverse problem: each bundle of M=5 Poisson intensities sums unlabeled photon contributions from K=3 line integrals. Because the measurement sums exponentials rather than forming one Beer-Lambert product, log and Σ do not commute and the inversion is nonlinear. We quantify the dose cost this multiplexing imposes and how closely estimators approach that limit.Approach. We treat the 5×3 bundle as a model problem for multiplexed photon aggregation, with TCT the motivating instance. Closed-form Cramér-Rao bounds (CRBs) are expressed as dose-inflation factors against an equal-dose single-source floor, and two estimators-a converged constrained maximum-likelihood estimator and a physics-motivated residual network-are benchmarked on synthetic independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.), analytical-phantom and single-patient bundles.Main results. Aggregation imposes a structural loss: at equal attenuation only 43% of single-source Fisher information survives for the endpoint paths and 23% for the middle path, fixing constant CRB inflation ratios √(7/3)≈1.53 and √(13/3)≈2.08. The constrained maximum-likelihood estimate attains the endpoint CRBs within a few percent but stays up to 1.35× above the middle-path bound. A learned prior narrows this gap where the middle path is photon-starved: on i.i.d. data the network cuts the constrained estimate's error by 27-49% for line-integral values of 6-9, nearly matching the Bayes posterior mean's overall error; on one patient, across separate body regions, it gains comparably for values of 5-8, loses elsewhere, and never falls below the equal-dose floor.Significance. The structure (a Poisson sum of exponentials) and methodology (Fisher-information efficiencies, dose-inflation accounting) are not specific to TCT: they characterize any measurement that aggregates attenuated photons before counting, transferring with only the incidence matrix respecified. Whether a learned prior yields a generalizable dose reduction is the open question a companion paper addresses through a multi-patient corpus.

articles.title: Butterfly vertebral body with spinal epidermoid cyst: a rare case report and review of the literature.
articles.abstract: Butterfly vertebrae and congenital spinal epidermoid cysts are embryonic spinal disorders, and their occurrence is closely related to tissue remnants during embryonic development. Notably, although both conditions are extremely rare, they may occur simultaneously in clinical practice, suggesting a possible, albeit hypothetical, spatiotemporal correlation in their embryonic origin-that is, developmental abnormalities during the somite differentiation and process of neural tube closure in the 3rd to 5th gestational weeks may simultaneously affect the formation of mesodermal vertebrae and the separation of ectodermal tissues. We report a rare case of concurrent T12 butterfly vertebra deformity and intradural extramedullary epidermoid cyst at the same spinal level, and explore their potential embryological correlation. A 43-year-old female with progressive lower extremity weakness and low back pain underwent imaging (X-ray, CT, MRI) confirming T12 butterfly vertebra and a spinal canal mass. Surgical intervention included posterior laminectomy, cyst resection, and spinal fixation. Histopathology confirmed epidermoid cyst diagnosis. To the best of our knowledge, this study reports the first case of concurrent butterfly vertebra (mesodermal origin) and spinal epidermoid cyst (ectodermal origin) at the same vertebral level. This unique coexistence provides a distinctive paradigm for investigating mesodermal-ectodermal interactions during spinal development. Identifying butterfly vertebrae warrants intraspinal screening for coexisting developmental anomalies to prevent potential irreversible neurological deficits.

articles.title: Glycerin suppositories as inexpensive multi-sequence MRI skin markers.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To assess MRI conspicuity and clinical usability of a commercially available glycerin suppository as a low-cost skin marker for musculoskeletal MRI across routine sequences. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A glycerin suppository was compared in vivo with vitamin E, water, olive oil, and diluted gadoteric acid solution across routine musculoskeletal MRI sequences. Conspicuity was scored independently by two musculoskeletal radiologists on a 4-point ordinal scale. Clinical usability was retrospectively assessed in 130 examinations at 1.5 and 3 T. One fat-sensitive image set (conventional T1-weighted or Dixon fat-only) and one fluid-sensitive set were scored independently by two readers. Scores of 2 or higher defined usability. Inter-reader agreement was assessed with Cohen kappa. RESULTS: Experimentally, the glycerin suppository showed the most consistent multi-sequence visibility among the tested markers. Unlike vitamin E markers, it remained highly conspicuous on fat-suppressed T1-weighted, fat-suppressed T2-weighted, and Dixon water-only images; it remained visible on STIR but showed lower conspicuity on Dixon fat-only images. Packaging did not affect visibility. Clinically, the marker was usable on both image sets in 123/130 examinations (94.6%) for reader 1 and 120/130 (92.3%) for reader 2. Usability on conventional T1-weighted images was 100% for both readers but decreased on Dixon fat-only reconstructions to 80.0% and 66.7%, respectively. Weighted kappa was 0.90 for fat-sensitive and 0.88 for fluid-sensitive scores. No marker-related image-quality degradation occurred. CONCLUSION: Glycerin suppositories are inexpensive, disposable MRI skin markers with broad sequence visibility. Their limitation is reduced conspicuity on Dixon fat-only reconstructions.

articles.title: Altered mechanical and vascular responses of the Achilles tendon to acute loading in Kendo athletes.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to elucidate acute, bilateral Achilles tendon (AT) responses to high-intensity single-leg hopping in Kendo athletes and healthy controls. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Twenty Kendo athletes and 20 sedentary controls performed a single-leg hopping task. Ultrasound imaging assessed AT anteroposterior diameter (APD), shear wave velocity (SWV), and intratendinous vessel count before (PRE), immediately after (POST), and 5-min post-exercise (POST5). RESULTS: Following exercise, Kendo athletes exhibited a significant main effect of time for both APD (P = 0.012) and SWV (P = 0.012), regardless of side. No significant acute changes in APD or SWV were observed in the control group. For intratendinous vascularity, a significant side-by-time interaction was observed in Kendo athletes (P = 0.026): the right leg showed no significant change, whereas the left leg exhibited a progressive increase from PRE to POST (P < 0.001) and further increased at POST5 (P = 0.002). In the control group, vessel count significantly increased at POST (P = 0.023) but rapidly returned to baseline. In the three-way analyses, no significant Group × Side × Time interaction was observed for any imaging outcome. CONCLUSION: Within Kendo athletes, morphological and mechanical responses occurred bilaterally, whereas the temporal vascular response differed between the left and right Achilles tendons. However, this side-specific vascular pattern was not shown to differ significantly from that observed in sedentary controls.

articles.title: MRI features of symptomatic progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy: a prospective cohort study using a standardized multisequence 3T MRI protocol.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) is an opportunistic infection of the brain caused by the JC polyomavirus (JCPyV). Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the most sensitive imaging modality for the in vivo detection of PML. However, comprehensive data on imaging findings using standardized multisequence MRI protocols are limited. OBJECTIVE: To systematically characterize MRI findings of clinically active PML in a large, prospectively collected cohort using a comprehensive and standardized MRI protocol. METHODS: Eighty patients with active PML underwent standardized 3T brain MRI including 3D T2w-fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR), 3D T1w, T2w, diffusion-weighted (DWI), susceptibility-weighted (SWI) and contrast-enhanced T1w sequences. Lesions were analysed for dissemination, location, morphology, borders, and signal characteristics. RESULTS: Most patients showed widespread (90%) and bilateral (93%) involvement. The frontal (91%) and parieto-occipital (93%) lobes were most frequently affected, with lesions typically involving the juxtacortical (95%) and deep white matter (99%), but also frequently extending into the cortical grey matter (94%) and deep grey matter (71%). Most patients showed large (> 3 cm, 89%), focal (99%), T2w-hyperintense (100%) and T1w-hypointense (99%) lesions with ill-defined borders (79%). DWI hyperintensity was present in 90% of patients, while hypointense (sub)cortical bands on SWI were detected in 61%. Contrast enhancement was observed in 55% of patients. Additional characteristic imaging features included the punctate pattern (76%) and the shrimp sign (20%). CONCLUSIONS: PML exhibits characteristic but heterogeneous MRI findings at the patient level, predominantly characterized by widespread white matter involvement with frequent cortical grey matter involvement. DWI and SWI frequently reveal additional characteristic imaging features that may aid in the identification and characterization of PML lesions. Our data support the use of standardized, comprehensive multisequence imaging protocols for consistent detection and phenotyping of PML across diverse immunosuppressive conditions.

articles.title: Preprocedural angiographic difference in cerebral circulation time and clinical outcomes after successful reperfusion for middle cerebral artery occlusion.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To investigate whether the affected-to-contralateral difference in cerebral circulation time (ΔCCT) on preprocedural digital subtraction angiography is associated with early neurological and 90-day functional outcomes after endovascular treatment (EVT) and successful reperfusion. METHODS: Patients with acute M1 or non-distal M2 middle cerebral artery occlusion who underwent EVT and achieved successful reperfusion (mTICI ≥2b) were retrospectively included. Semi-automatically measured ΔCCT was evaluated in relation to the primary outcome of 24-hour National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) improvement and the exploratory outcomes of early neurological deterioration (END) and a 90-day modified Rankin Scale (mRS) score ≥ 3. Models were adjusted for age, sex, baseline NIHSS score, collateral status, and occlusion location. RESULTS: Among 132 patients, the median ΔCCT was 1.31 s (IQR, 0.97-1.67 s). Each 1-standard-deviation increase in ΔCCT was associated with 3.39 points less 24-hour NIHSS improvement (adjusted β = -3.39, 95% confidence interval [CI] -4.79 to -1.98; P < 0.001), higher odds of END (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 3.11, 95% CI 1.92-5.42; P < 0.001), and higher odds of a 90-day mRS score ≥ 3 (aOR 1.58, 95% CI 1.06-2.41; P = 0.028). CONCLUSION: Among patients with M1 or non-distal M2 occlusion who achieved successful reperfusion, a longer pre-EVT ΔCCT was associated with less early neurological improvement and, in exploratory analyses, higher odds of END and an unfavorable 90-day outcome. Its generalizability to broader EVT populations requires further evaluation.

articles.title: Deep learning pulmonary vessel segmentation for contrast-enhanced and non-contrast CT images.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Accurate and comprehensive segmentation of pulmonary vasculature is essential for diagnosing various pulmonary diseases and lung surgical planning. PURPOSE: To develop a deep learning model for pulmonary vessels segmentation based on both computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA) and non-contrast computed tomography (NCCT) data, and to evaluate its performance on a clinical dataset. METHODS: In this retrospective study, we collected 427 cases of chest CT data from different countries and manufacturers, including 213 CTPA cases and 214 NCCT cases. And we designed a CTPA and NCCT ground truth (GT) generation method producing high-accuracy vessel annotation dataset. Then we developed a 3D U-Net based deep learning method with the Vessel Lumen Structure Optimization Module (VLSOM). We numerically evaluated model using metrics including Centerline Recall (Cl-Recall), Centerline DICE (Cl-DICE), Average Symmetric Surface Distance (ASSD) and 95% Hausdorff Distance (HD95) focusing on the integrity of vascular structures. Finally, the model performance was visually assessed in an independent external dataset. RESULTS: In the numerical evaluation on the internal test dataset with 57 cases, our model achieved Cl-DICE, Cl-Recall and HD95 values of 0.909 (95% CI [0.904, 0.914]), 0.883 (95% CI [0.873, 0.891]) and 1.861 mm (95% CI [1.674 mm, 2.073 mm]) which is superior to the state of the art (SOTA) baseline model nnU-Net v2 of 0.860 (95% CI [0.852, 0.867]), 0.772 (95% CI [0.760, 0.783])and 2.458 mm (95% CI [2.219 mm, 2.708 mm]) (all p < 0.001). In the clinical visual assessments on the 90 sets of external datasets, the average score for accuracy and robustness, branch abundance, computer-aided detection and vascular continuity 4.52 (95% CI [4.42, 4.62]), 4.82 (95% CI [4.76, 4.90]), 4.58 (95% CI [4.46, 4.69]), and 4.85 (95% CI [4.77, 4.92]) respectively with a full score of 5. CONCLUSIONS: The proposed pulmonary vessel segmentation algorithm performed well in preserving the connectivity and integrity of the vascular structure on both CTPA and NCCT data with various diseases. CRITICAL RELEVANCE STATEMENT: A vessel centerline topology-enhanced deep segmentation model enables accurate and automatic pulmonary vessel segmentation in both computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA) and non-contrast computed tomography (NCCT) images.

articles.title: Toward a unified computational representation of lung cancer: from radiomics and pathomics to multimodal AI.
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how lung cancer is characterized by enabling quantitative analysis of both radiologic and pathologic images. Radiomics extracts high-dimensional features from radiologic images, whereas pathomics applies analogous approaches to digitized histopathology, providing complementary representations of tumor biology across different spatial scales. Recent advances in foundation models and multimodal AI have accelerated the convergence of these disciplines, creating opportunities to integrate imaging, pathology, and molecular information within unified frameworks. In this review, we summarize the principles of radiomics and pathomics, discuss recent developments in foundation models for thoracic imaging and computational pathology, and examine emerging strategies for multimodal integration in lung cancer. Available evidence, although largely retrospective, suggests that integrated radio-pathomic models can outperform single-modality approaches for clinically complex tasks, including recurrence prediction, molecular characterization, and treatment response assessment. We also discuss the major barriers limiting clinical translation, including reproducibility, external validation, interoperability, interpretability, and regulatory implementation. Rather than replacing radiology or pathology, multimodal AI is progressively connecting both disciplines through shared computational representations of disease, supporting more comprehensive and biologically informed approaches to precision oncology.

articles.title: Myelin water fraction mapping with voxelwise appraisal of solution ambiguity by globally optimized single and joint inversion of spin- and gradient-echo data.
articles.abstract: Quantitative mapping of the myelin water fraction (MWF) is a key objective in neuroimaging, yet the ambiguity of MWF estimates arising from ill-posed inversion problems is rarely assessed at the voxel level. We propose a global-search inversion framework based on particle swarm optimization (PSO) for single and joint inversion of multi-echo MRI data (T2 and T2*) without additional regularization of the individual inverse problems. Repeated PSO runs per voxel yield ensembles of solutions that enable an empirical appraisal of near-optimal solution variability under the chosen model assumptions and misfit criterion. Simulation results show accurate recovery of MWF under the investigated conditions and demonstrate how joint inversion can constrain the solution space. In vivo experiments reveal differences between T2- and T2*-based MWF estimates, with variations across subjects. Joint inversion yields compromise solutions, while preserving sensitivity to inter-contrast discrepancies. The proposed framework complements conventional MWF imaging by providing voxelwise information on the variability of near-optimal solutions, offering a basis for evaluating inversion stability and solution ambiguity.

articles.title: Triple-rule-out computed tomography (CT) angiography revisited: selective contemporary use enabled by sequential acquisition and modern cardiovascular computed tomography (CT).
articles.abstract: Triple-rule-out computed tomography angiography (TRO-CTA) was introduced to evaluate acute coronary syndrome (ACS), pulmonary embolism (PE), and acute aortic syndrome (AAS) in a single emergency department (ED) examination. Early single-pass protocols were limited by compromise bolus timing, retrospective gating over a long z-axis, high radiation and iodine burden, and inconsistent coronary image quality, and routine use appropriately declined as dedicated coronary CT angiography (CCTA) and high-sensitivity troponin algorithms matured. A subset of patients nevertheless remains difficult to triage: older or multimorbid patients with overlapping symptoms, nonspecific troponin or D-dimer elevation, or limited access to subspecialty interpretation. Wide-detector and high-pitch acquisition, low-tube-voltage imaging, iterative and deep-learning reconstruction, and artificial intelligence (AI)-based motion correction have reduced the penalties that constrained early protocols, and sequential multiphase acquisition images each territory within its own enhancement window from one coordinated injection. This review reappraises TRO-CTA from a contemporary cardiovascular CT perspective. Dedicated coronary, pulmonary, or aortic CTA remains preferred when one diagnosis is dominant, and selective TRO-CTA is confined to stable patients with persistent diagnostic ambiguity after first-tier evaluation. For contemporary sequential multiphase TRO-CTA, evidence remains largely limited to single-center feasibility and image-quality studies; robust prospective comparative data on diagnostic timeliness, missed diagnoses, downstream testing, and clinical outcomes remain lacking. Value is additionally context-dependent, varying with ED case-mix, scanner platform, availability of expert interpretation, local disease prevalence, and access to staged reassessment. Contemporary TRO-CTA is therefore a selective, institution-calibrated option requiring explicit activation criteria, demonstrated coronary image quality, and prospective multicenter evaluation.

articles.title: Commentary: preparing radiologists for an artificial intelligence-enabled future.
Transvaginal ultrasound-based deep learning radiomics for preoperative identification of non-endometrioid endometrial carcinoma: A multicenter study.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Preoperative identification of non-endometrioid endometrial carcinoma (NEEC) is clinically important because non-endometrioid histology may influence risk assessment and treatment planning. This study aimed to develop and externally validate a transvaginal ultrasound-based deep learning radiomics (DLR) model for preoperative identification of NEEC. METHODS: A total of 663 patients with pathologically confirmed endometrial carcinoma from 11 centers were retrospectively included. The training cohort consisted of 483 patients from eight centers, including 161 NEEC and 322 EEC cases. An independent external test cohort included 180 patients from three additional centers, including 60 NEEC and 120 EEC cases. Radiomics features were extracted using PyRadiomics, and deep learning features were extracted using ResNet-101. Radiomics, deep learning, and combined DLR models were developed using machine learning classifiers and evaluated by receiver operating characteristic analysis, calibration curves, decision curve analysis, and external validation. RESULTS: The combined DLR model achieved the best diagnostic performance among the three models. In the external test cohort, the DLR model yielded an AUC of 0.837, with an accuracy of 0.756, sensitivity of 0.800, and specificity of 0.733. The DLR model outperformed the radiomics model and the deep learning model in both the training and external test cohorts. CONCLUSION: The transvaginal ultrasound-based DLR model showed potential as a noninvasive tool for preoperative identification of NEEC. This model may provide complementary information for individualized preoperative assessment, although prospective validation is required before clinical implementation.

articles.title: Ultrasound non-mass lesions of the breast: imaging features, pathologic risk, and interobserver agreement.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: This study aimed to evaluate the sonographic and clinical characteristics of breast non-mass lesions detected on ultrasound, identify factors associated with increasing pathological risk, and assess interobserver agreement among breast radiologists. METHODS: This retrospective study included breast ultrasound examinations performed between January 1, 2021, and August 30, 2025. A keyword search in the picture archiving and communication system identified 2,002 examinations potentially describing non-mass findings. After exclusions, 666 potentially eligible lesions were independently evaluated by three breast radiologists. Lesions were classified as non-mass according to a predefined majority rule (≥ 2 of 3 observers) and assessed using a three-level clinical concern score. Final diagnoses were established by histopathology or ≥ 2 years of imaging follow-up. Associations between imaging and clinical variables and pathological categories were evaluated using univariable analyses and multivariable ordinal logistic regression. Interobserver agreement was assessed using kappa statistics and Gwet's AC1. RESULTS: A total of 610 lesions in 610 patients were classified as non-mass by majority decision. Malignancy was identified in 13 of 610 lesions (2.1%). Interobserver agreement for non-mass classification was high, although agreement estimates differed between Gwet's AC1 (0.80) and Fleiss' kappa (0.24). A clinical concern score of 3 predicted malignancy with a sensitivity of 76.9% (10/13) and specificity of 98.6% (582/590). Multivariable analysis showed that architectural distortion [odds ratio (OR): 8.40; 95% confidence interval (CI): 3.89-18.16; P < 0.001], posterior acoustic shadowing (OR: 4.76; 95% CI: 1.84-12.28; P = 0.001), and vascularity (OR: 2.69; 95% CI: 1.22-5.97; P = 0.015) were independently associated with increasing pathological risk. CONCLUSION: Most breast non-mass lesions detected on ultrasound are benign; however, architectural distortion, posterior acoustic shadowing, and vascularity are independently associated with increased pathological risk. CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE: Recognizing specific ultrasound features associated with higher pathological risk may help distinguish non-mass lesions requiring more intensive diagnostic evaluation from predominantly benign findings and support more consistent clinical management.

articles.title: Predictive factors for non-diagnostic results of computed tomography-guided percutaneous core needle biopsy of the lung: focus on computed tomography findings.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Computed tomography (CT)-guided percutaneous core needle biopsy (PCNB) of pulmonary lesions is widely used for tissue diagnosis, but non-diagnostic results remain common and can delay diagnosis, prompting repeat biopsy or prolonged follow-up. This study aimed to identify clinical, CT, and procedural predictors of non-diagnostic PCNB results and to develop a scoring system for risk stratification. METHODS: This retrospective study included consecutive CT-guided PCNBs performed for pulmonary lesions at a single tertiary center between January 2019 and March 2021, comprising 358 PCNBs in the training cohort and 126 in the validation cohort. Clinical, radiologic, and procedural variables were compared between diagnostic and non-diagnostic groups. Independent predictors were identified using multivariate logistic regression with Firth's penalized likelihood method to reduce small-sample bias, and a weighted scoring system was developed. Discriminative performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). RESULTS: Non-diagnostic rates were 20.4% (73/358) and 22.2% (28/126) in the training and validation cohorts, respectively; 34.7% of non-diagnostic results were ultimately confirmed as malignant. Five independent predictors of non-diagnostic results were identified: lesion size ≤ 1.5 cm [odds ratio (OR), 2.434; 95% confidence interval (CI), 1.111-5.204], patchy morphology (OR, 2.423; 95% CI, 1.210-4.794), atelectasis adjacent to the target lesion (OR, 2.221; 95% CI, 1.096-4.426), absence of pleural invasion (OR, 8.418; 95% CI, 2.084-77.273), and inaccurate needle tip positioning (OR, 3.669; 95% CI, 1.513-8.907). The scoring system demonstrated modest discriminative performance in the training (AUC, 0.731; bootstrap optimism-corrected AUC, 0.692) and validation cohorts (AUC, 0.769), with a stepwise increase in non-diagnostic probability across four score-based risk groups. CONCLUSION: Lesion size ≤ 1.5 cm, patchy morphology, atelectasis adjacent to the target lesion, absence of pleural invasion, and inaccurate needle tip positioning were independent predictors of non-diagnostic results after CT-guided PCNB. The derived scoring system showed consistent performance in a temporal validation cohort. CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE: The derived scoring system, based on readily assessable CT and procedural factors, may enable pre-procedural risk stratification, facilitate individualized biopsy planning, optimize sampling strategy, and improve diagnostic yield.

articles.title: Multiparametric Transperineal Ultrasound Features of Perianal Fistulas in Pediatric Crohn's Disease: From Baseline to Radiologic Healing.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To evaluate and compare the multiparametric transperineal ultrasound (TPUS) features of perianal fistulas at baseline and upon achieving magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-confirmed radiologic healing in pediatric Crohn disease. METHODS: This retrospective study included 24 children (22 boys and 2 girls; mean age, 13.0 ± 2.3 years [range, 9-19]) with 45 perianal fistulas evaluated between January 2019 and July 2025. All patients with fistulas who underwent at least 2 TPUS and pelvic MRI assessments and achieved complete healing on MRI were enrolled. Baseline and follow-up TPUS images were evaluated in consensus by 2 radiologists for multiple parameters, including diameter, echogenicity relative to the internal anal sphincter (IAS), vascularity, internal pattern (layered versus homogeneous), anisotropy, presence of pus, air bubbles, abscesses, and adjacent inflammation. Changes in these findings were compared using paired t-tests and McNemar tests. RESULTS: At baseline (n = 45), most fistulas demonstrated higher echogenicity than that of the IAS (73%), exhibited a layered pattern (80%) and internal vascularity (94%) and frequently showed pus (40%) and adjacent inflammation (78%). Despite achieving complete MRI-defined radiologic healing, perianal fistulas remained detectable by TPUS in the majority of cases (60%, 27/45), while the other 18 fistulas (40%) were no longer detectable. However, the 27 persisting fistulas demonstrated significant multiparametric evolution, including reductions in diameter (p < .001), loss of the layered pattern (p < .001), increased anisotropy (p < .001), decreased vascularity (p = .002), and resolution of pus (p = .001) and adjacent inflammation (p < .001). CONCLUSION: Radiologic healing in pediatric perianal Crohn disease is characterized by distinct multiparametric TPUS changes, including diameter reduction, loss of layered pattern, emergence of anisotropy, and resolution of inflammatory markers. While TPUS serves as a valuable adjunct to MRI for assessing treatment response, the persistent sonographic detectability of fistulas despite MRI-defined healing warrants further validation in larger cohorts and long-term follow-up studies.
